tEn: Why MCP and Tools Are Obsolete: The Future of AI Is Direct Code Interaction
tZh: 为什么 MCP 和工具调用已经过时：AI 的未来是直接与代码交互
sEn: A candid take on why tool-calling architectures like MCP are unnecessary, and a personal story of how a 2015 Karpathy article led to a startup failure and eventual vindication with ChatGPT.
sZh: 坦诚分享为什么 MCP 这类工具调用架构是多余的，以及一段因 2015 年 Karpathy 文章而创业失败、最终被 ChatGPT 验证的个人经历。

consensus.en: Model building is 90% engineering; an industrialized end-to-end model factory lets small teams compress training-to-launch cycles to weeks.
consensus.zh: 模型构建 90% 是工程；端到端的工业化“模型工厂”让小型团队能把从训练到发布的周期压缩到几周。

consensus.en: Reinforcement learning is the main driver of post-training capability; persistence and verification behavior can unlock far more from smaller models.
consensus.zh: 强化学习是后训练能力的主要驱动；持久性和验证性行为能从较小模型中解锁远多于此前的性能。

consensus.en: Scaling up frontier models is still necessary; openness and commoditization do not eliminate the need to scale to compete.
consensus.zh: 扩张前沿模型仍然是必要的；开放与商品化并不会消除为了竞争而进行 Scaling 的必要性。

consensus.en: The web holds far more learnable knowledge than plain next-token prediction extracts; future pre-training will add reinforcement learning earlier and better curricula.
consensus.zh: 网络蕴含的可学习知识远超单纯的下一个词预测所能提取；未来的预训练会更早引入强化学习和更优的课程安排。

consensus.en: Many independent foundation-model labs should exist; sharing research and giving users choice matters more than a handful of dominant companies.
consensus.zh: 应当存在许多独立的基础模型实验室；共享研究、给用户选择，比少数几家主导公司更重要。

consensus.en: The race is measured by calendar time, not GPU count; reproducibility and reliable infrastructure let small teams iterate faster.
consensus.zh: 这场竞赛以日历时间计，而非 GPU 数量；可复现性与可靠基础设施让小型团队迭代更快。

contrarian.en: MCP and tool-calling layers are stupid; models should directly write and run code in a minimal virtual machine instead.
contrarian.zh: MCP 和工具调用层是愚蠢的；模型应该直接编写并运行代码，而不是塞满工具调用。

contrarian.en: The training run is not the expensive part; cumulative R&D, data, and infrastructure cost are what open-weight labs really pay.
contrarian.zh: 训练运行本身并不是最贵的部分；累计研发、数据和基础设施成本才是开放权重实验室真正付出的代价。

contrarian.en: The optimal model size for most knowledge work may be near trillion scale, not two or three orders of magnitude larger.
contrarian.zh: 大多数知识工作的最优模型规模可能接近万亿参数级，而不是再大两三个数量级。

contrarian.en: RL time, not GPU count, is the wall-clock bottleneck in post-training because batch size is constrained; hardware disaggregation can help.
contrarian.zh: 后训练中的墙上时钟瓶颈是强化学习时间，而非 GPU 数量，因为批量大小受限；硬件拆分能改善这一点。

contrarian.en: Blanket restrictions on open-weight models rightly worry incumbents, but they can entrench an oligopoly just like the cigarette-ad ban.
contrarian.zh: 对开放权重模型的一刀切限制确实令人担忧，但它可能像香烟广告禁令一样固化寡头格局。

contrarian.en: Distilling from a huge unreleased teacher is not always right; frequent from-scratch training yields clearer scientific experiments and insights.
contrarian.zh: 从巨大的未发布教师模型蒸馏未必是对的；频繁从零开始训练能带来更清晰的科学实验和洞察。

turns.en: Now three years ago that wasn't fully obvious yet. I think today that very much is. And we also realized that some of the world's most capable people with the most interesting innovative ideas were not just going to be here. And so it led us to create a fully remote company. We ended up opening an office in Paris and London and different places. We have a lot of the team in the US and a lot outside, but we always took the view that we're an American company, but if we want the best of the best to work with us, we need to take a global view. We do also have people here in Silicon Valley as the company's grown, but I think one of the things that slowed us down at the beginning has sped us up now. It's why you're seeing the progress on our models and the cadence at which we release. Because we didn't spin out of an existing lab. We didn't actually have a lot of the information that's freely flowing around here at the time. We just took this point of view: okay, let's work the problem, let's read the few papers that are out there, and let's figure this stuff out. And we made some hilarious mistakes in model training because of that over the years, especially in the first 12 months. There are a few that I think still haunt me and scare me. We can talk about them later. But it created a resiliency and persistency in the team. Extremely few people have left us over the years, and that told us, okay, we can do this. When we first wrote our first training codebase completely from scratch, it wasn't a fork of any open source. It was like, okay, let's build it from scratch. I remember we had this one moment where we spent three weeks working out an optimizer bug. Training just couldn't get stable. We obsessed over it and thought maybe we were wrong, maybe we should have forked this repo. But then when we solved it, I still remember at the time we were five people in the company. When we solved it, we thought, oh, we can do things if we're just willing to work hard. I think that culture with a very strong engineering bias has helped us get to where we are. And so there's this notion of open source and talent and these things. I think we just took different decisions from a different starting point. I think we are lucky. I do want to definitely call it lucky, but also a lot of hard work of the team that now is starting to show up in results.
turns.zh: 三年前，这一点还不完全明显。我觉得今天已经非常明显了。我们还意识到，世界上最能干、想法最创新的一些人不会只待在这里。所以这促使我们创建了一家完全远程的公司。我们最终在巴黎、伦敦和其他地方开设了办公室。我们有很多团队成员在美国，也有很多在美国以外，但我们一直持这样的观点：我们是一家美国公司，但如果我们想和最优秀的人合作，就需要放眼全球。随着公司发展，我们在硅谷也确实有人，但我认为有一件事起初拖慢了我们的速度，现在却加快了我们的速度。这就是为什么你会看到我们模型的进展和发布节奏。因为我们不是从现有实验室孵化出来的。当时我们实际上没有大量这里自由流动的信息。我们只是持这样的观点：好，那就解决问题吧，读读那几篇论文，自己搞清楚。多年来，我们在模型训练中因此犯了一些荒唐的错误，尤其是在头 12 个月。有几个错误我想起来仍然心有余悸。我们以后可以聊聊这些。但它给团队带来了一种韧性和坚持。这些年来离开我们的人极少，这告诉我们：好的，我们能行。当我们第一次完全从头编写训练代码库时，它不是任何开源项目的分支。我们想的是：好，从头开始造。我记得有一次我们花了三周时间排查一个优化器（optimizer）的 bug，训练就是无法稳定下来。我们痴迷于这个问题，甚至怀疑自己是不是错了，也许应该直接 fork 那个代码库。但当我们最终解决后——我仍然记得当时公司只有五个人——我们想，哦，只要我们愿意努力，就能做事。我认为这种带有极强工程导向的文化帮助我们走到了今天。所以关于开源、人才这些概念，我觉得我们只是从不同的起点做了不同的决定。我认为我们很幸运。我当然要把这称为运气，但也离不开团队的大量努力，现在这些努力开始体现在成果上。

turns.en: Just because we probably won't revisit this again, but this is a fun recruiting challenge if someone knows the answer. What was the bug? And we won't tell the solution.
turns.zh: 正好因为我们可能不会再聊这个了，但这是一个有趣的招聘挑战，如果有人知道答案的话。那个 bug 是什么？我们不会公布答案。

turns.en: So the bug... You're going to test my memory here. But I think I can recall. So if you take Adam as an optimizer, you have epsilon, which is right in the denominator. At the time, if I recall, you looked at the early LLaMA papers and things like that. People were juicing epsilon quite a bit. They were adding, I don't know if it was 1e-4 or whatever, a high value for epsilon. And if you think about this during training, it's kind of weird and counterintuitive that we're adding noise to our optimizer by just adding effectively a random number in the denominator, right behind the decimal point. And I don't recall the exact bug, but what I remember is once we solved it, we no longer had to juice epsilon as much as was happening in the LLaMA paper and other places. It was one of those fundamental moments where we had trusted this paper that was out there and thought, oh no, it has to be this way, it has to have this high value of epsilon. But it made no sense to us intuitively. Why do you have to have it so high? If you're just trying to avoid division by zero, why can't the value be extremely small? That was one of those moments where you realize that finding things out from scratch yourself builds a better intuition, because the one thing you learn very quickly with model building is that your initial intuitions are going to get beaten up so hard. It's such an experimental science. The things that seem obvious, you quickly learn you were wrong. Hopefully you figure out why, and sometimes you don't even.
turns.zh: 这个 bug 嘛……你这是要考我的记忆力。不过我想我能回忆起来。如果你以 Adam 作为优化器，你会有一个 epsilon，它在分母里。当时，如果我没记错的话，你看了早期的 LLaMA 论文之类的。大家把 epsilon 调得相当高，他们加了一个不知道是不是 1e-4 的高值。如果你想想训练过程中的这个操作，会觉得有点奇怪和反直觉：我们在分母里加一个有效随机数，就给优化器引入了噪声。我不记得确切的问题了，但我记得的是，一旦我们解决了它，我们就不再需要像 LLaMA 论文里那样把 epsilon 调得那么高了。那是那些根本性时刻之一：我们相信了那篇论文，以为哦不，就必须这样，必须用这么高的 epsilon。但直觉上完全说不通：为什么要这么高？如果你只是想避免除以零，为什么不能把值设得极低？那是你会意识到的时刻之一：自己从头摸索会建立更好的直觉，因为你在构建模型时很快学到的第一件事就是，你最初的直觉会被狠狠打击。这是一门实验科学，那些看似显然的事，你很快会发现自己错了，希望你能找到原因，有时候甚至找不到。

turns.en: Um yeah, so you know, one of the reasons that when you released your new models, Vivoo got really excited. I mean, everyone got really excited, but Vivu led our paper club on it, and you guys saw it obviously. Maybe talk through some lessons learned in that. Whatever you can sort of disclose. We can focus on model factory stuff, whatever you think is a good starting point.
turns.zh: 嗯，是的。所以你知道，当你发布新模型的时候，Vivoo 非常兴奋。我是说，每个人都很兴奋，但 Vivu 在我们的论文俱乐部里主导了这件事，你们显然也看到了。也许可以聊聊其中的一些经验教训。你能透露多少就透露多少。我们可以聚焦于模型工厂（model factory）相关的东西，你觉得哪个起点合适都行。

turns.en: So I would say that our view from very early on in the company was that model building is ultimately 90% engineering. I think we all know it in the industry, because if you look at where every researcher is spending their time, they're spending their time writing code, looking at data, and writing code. So we said, okay, the state at the moment, like 3 years ago, was bash scripts and Slurm and spaghetti code bases for training, and data pipelines that were kind of patched together. We looked at this and said, ultimately model building is a process. You're going from raw data—pre-training raw material like the web—doing a whole bunch of filtering, cleaning up, transformations, analyzing. These days it's far more complex than it was 3 years ago. Then you're training a model, which is effectively a large distributed systems problem across hardware that has become a lot more reliable but was extremely flaky back then. Now with every new generation we get new sets of challenges. Then you go into the next stages—there was no mid-training back then—but you go to post-training and then reinforcement learning. So we looked at this and said, well, this looks like an industrialized process, an end-to-end process, where every single part has its machinery, whether it's your big data pipelines, your crawling ingestion of the web, or your large-scale distributed training, and then you have your reliability.
turns.zh: 我想说，我们公司很早就有一个观点：模型构建最终 90% 是工程问题。我认为这在我们行业是共识，因为如果你看看每个研究人员的时间花在哪里，他们总是在写代码、看数据、写代码。所以我们当时说，好的，3 年前的状态是 bash 脚本、Slurm、用于训练的面条式代码库，以及拼凑起来的数据管道。我们看到这些后说，模型构建本质上是一个流水线。你从原始数据开始——预训练的原材料，比如互联网——然后做大量的过滤、清洗、转换、分析。如今这比 3 年前复杂得多。然后你训练模型，这实际上是一个大型分布式系统问题，要跨硬件运行；硬件现在可靠多了，但当时极不稳定。现在每一代新模型都会给我们带来一系列新挑战。然后进入下一阶段——当时还没有中途训练——但你会做后训练，然后是强化学习。所以我们看完后说，这看起来像一个工业化流程，一个端到端的流程，其中每个环节都有自己的机器：无论是大数据管道、网络爬取与摄入，还是大规模分布式训练，然后是可靠性。
